strengths: The core idea is appealing and practically relevant: training grasping policies on randomly composed primitive “toys” as a route to object generalization is simple, intuitive, and potentially useful for scalable robotic data collection.
The paper reports a reasonably broad empirical study for a manipulation paper, including simulation on YCB objects, real Franka experiments, and an additional humanoid/dexterous-hand setup.
The DetPool ablation is compelling within the presented experiments: object-centric attention masking plus pooling substantially outperforms mean, CLS, and attention pooling in simulation.
The paper includes useful scaling and design ablations, including number of demonstrations, number of toys, model size, primitive type, toy complexity, and color diversity.

The appendix provides many implementation and hardware details, including toy generation, 3D-printing parameters, teleoperation setup, training details, baseline training procedures, and evaluation protocols.
weaknesses: The main claims are somewhat overstated. In the real Franka results, fine-tuned pi0-FAST achieves 76.56% while the proposed method achieves 66.67%, yet the abstract and conclusion suggest the method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches relying on more data. The paper should state the comparison more carefully.

The dependence on object masks is a major unresolved issue. In simulation, ground-truth masks are used; in real experiments, the method relies on a trained detector plus SAM 2. The paper does not adequately analyze mask quality, detector failures, sensitivity to segmentation errors, or how target object masks are obtained in cluttered or multi-object settings.

Baseline comparisons are not fully convincing. Large VLA models may be disadvantaged by small-data fine-tuning, action/control mismatches, different camera inputs, checkpoint selection choices, and embodiment mismatch. The paper reports poor VLA performance but does not establish that these baselines were tuned as strongly as the proposed architecture.

The task scope is narrow: single-step grasp-and-lift evaluation with known object placement grids. It is unclear how well the approach transfers to clutter, occlusion, multi-object selection, articulated objects, deformables, task-conditioned grasping, or longer-horizon manipulation.

The real-world evaluation lacks statistical uncertainty. Success rates are reported without confidence intervals, significance tests, per-object breakdown for the main Franka/YCB setting, or analysis of failure modes.

The novelty of DetPool is incremental relative to prior object-centric and segmentation-based visual pooling methods. The more novel aspect is the primitive-toy training distribution, but the paper does not isolate whether gains come from toy composition, object-centric masking, data collection protocol, or architecture choices.

There are reproducibility gaps despite extensive appendices: the project page placeholder is blank in the manuscript, and it is not clear that code, checkpoints, meshes, masks, and demonstrations are actually available for independent verification.

Some experimental choices weaken interpretation, such as using ground-truth masks in simulation but learned masks in real settings, lowering the OpenVLA-OFT success threshold in simulation, and selecting early checkpoints for pi0-FAST in the H1-2 setting due to overfitting.

strengths: The paper studies an important problem in robotic manipulation: generalizing grasping behavior from limited training objects to novel real-world objects.
The idea of constructing training objects from simple geometric primitives is intuitive, practically appealing, and potentially useful as a data-generation strategy.
The paper includes both simulation and real-robot experiments, including a Franka setup and a humanoid dexterous-hand setup, which is more ambitious than many purely simulated manipulation papers.

The DetPool mechanism is simple and appears empirically useful in the authors' setup; the simulation ablation against mean, CLS, and attention pooling supports the importance of object-focused visual features.
The appendix contains useful implementation details about toy generation, 3D printing, robot setups, and evaluation protocols, which improves reproducibility relative to the main text alone.
weaknesses: The main claims are overstated. The abstract says the method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches relying on substantially more in-domain data, but in the real Franka results the finetuned pi0-FAST baseline substantially outperforms the proposed method. This directly weakens the central empirical narrative.

The novelty is limited. Training on primitive-composed objects and using object-centric masking/pooling are reasonable ideas, but the paper does not convincingly distinguish itself from prior object-centric grasping, grasp generalization, synthetic-object training, domain randomization, and geometric-shape abstraction work.

The evaluation is not strong enough to support the broad generalization claims. The method is tested mainly on grasping, a single-step task, and mostly on YCB-like tabletop objects. Claims about scalable general-purpose manipulation are much broader than the evidence.

The comparison to VLA baselines is hard to interpret. OpenVLA-OFT and pi0-FAST are not primarily designed for this exact low-data, single-task grasping setting, and the paper provides limited evidence that they were tuned comparably well. Their poor simulation results may reflect control/action-space or finetuning mismatch rather than a clear advantage of the proposed representation.

The method relies on object masks at test time: ground-truth masks in simulation and a detector plus SAM 2 in real settings. This is a significant external dependency and weakens the claim that the grasping policy itself has learned robust object-centric generalization. The cost, failure modes, and sensitivity of this perception pipeline are not sufficiently evaluated.

The real-world evaluation has important limitations. The Franka result is below finetuned pi0-FAST, and the H1-2 evaluation uses only 13 objects with 5 trials each, producing high variance and limited statistical reliability. No confidence intervals or significance tests are reported.

There is potential selection bias in the real-toy pipeline: the paper says it 3D-prints the 250 toys with the highest simulated success rates, which may make the training distribution easier and complicates the interpretation of generalization from random toys.

The ablations are incomplete. The paper does not isolate whether gains come from DetPool, the external segmentation/detection system, MVP pretraining, object cropping/masking more generally, toy diversity, color diversity, or model capacity in a sufficiently controlled way.

The benchmark baselines omit or underemphasize several relevant grasping methods and datasets, such as grasp synthesis, affordance-based grasping, GraspNet-style approaches, Dex-Net-style methods, and stronger object-centric manipulation baselines. ShapeGrasp alone is not enough to establish competitiveness against the grasping literature.

The paper's writing sometimes frames simple design choices as stronger conceptual contributions than warranted, including the cognitive-science analogy. The child-learning motivation is appealing but not actually validated experimentally.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and appealing idea: train grasping policies on randomly assembled primitive-shaped toys and test zero-shot transfer to real objects. The framing is intuitive and potentially useful for scalable robot data collection.

The empirical scope is stronger than many manipulation papers: results include simulation, a real Franka/YCB setup, and a humanoid dexterous-hand setting, with nontrivial success rates and comparisons to large VLA baselines.

The DetPool ablation is convincing within the presented setup. The gap over mean, CLS, and attention pooling in simulation is large, supporting the claim that object-centric visual representations are important for this type of generalization.

The paper includes several useful analyses on number of demonstrations, toy diversity, primitive type, toy complexity, color diversity, and model size, which makes the study more informative than a single benchmark result.

Reproducibility is reasonably addressed through implementation details, hardware descriptions, toy generation/manufacturing details, baseline training settings, and stated plans to release code, checkpoints, data, and videos.
weaknesses: The central generalization claim is somewhat weakened by reliance on external object localization/segmentation machinery. In simulation the method uses ground-truth masks, while in real experiments it uses a detector trained on manually annotated toy images plus SAM 2; this makes the policy less purely learned from random toys than the main narrative suggests.

The novelty of DetPool is limited: it is essentially segmentation-mask-constrained transformer attention followed by pooling. The paper would be stronger with deeper positioning against object-centric manipulation, cropping/ROI baselines, masked autoencoder variants, and methods such as OTTER beyond a brief discussion.

The real-world Franka headline should be stated more carefully. The method is second-best in Table 2 and is substantially below finetuned pi0-FAST, so claims of outperforming state-of-the-art models are only true for selected settings or zero-shot variants.

The evaluation is still narrow: all tasks are single-step grasp-and-lift, success is binary lift height, and there is little analysis of failure modes, object categories, material/geometry distributions, occlusion, clutter, or robustness to segmentation errors.

Some comparisons may not be fully apples-to-apples. Baselines use different camera inputs, action parameterizations, language prompts, checkpoint selection procedures, and training schedules; the paper does not provide enough evidence that the strong VLA baselines were optimally adapted to this unusual toy-training regime.

The real-robot evidence would benefit from confidence intervals or statistical testing. The H1-2 evaluation is especially small, with only five trials per object and acknowledged hardware issues, so its conclusions should be treated as suggestive rather than definitive.

The paper sometimes overstates biological motivation and broad implications. The cognitive-science analogy is inspiring, but the experimental evidence mainly supports a practical primitive-to-object grasping transfer recipe, not a strong claim about child-like learning mechanisms.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and appealing hypothesis: training grasping policies on procedurally composed primitive-shape toys can induce useful zero-shot generalization to real objects. This is a meaningful and well-motivated direction for scalable robotic data collection.

The empirical scope is stronger than many robotics submissions: the authors evaluate in simulation, on a real Franka setup with many YCB objects, and on a humanoid/dexterous-hand platform, with several ablations on data scale, toy diversity, primitive type, model size, robustness, and control choices.

The DetPool mechanism is simple, plausible, and well supported by ablations. The gap between DetPool and standard pooling methods is large in simulation, suggesting that object-centric visual representations are indeed important for this setting.

The toy generation and manufacturing details are unusually concrete, including primitive ranges, print settings, data collection protocols, and baseline implementation details, which improves reproducibility.

The result that relatively small robot-specific datasets can outperform or approach much larger VLA baselines on a narrow but important manipulation skill is potentially significant for robotic learning.
weaknesses: The central claims are somewhat overstated. The title and framing suggest learning to grasp broadly from toys, but the evaluated task is mostly single-step pick-and-lift grasping under controlled tabletop setups, with only one additional push task in the appendix.

The method relies heavily on object masks/detections at test time, including SAM 2 and a Faster R-CNN detector trained from manually annotated toy images. This makes the claimed simplicity and generality less clean, and the paper does not fully analyze failures or robustness when object localization is wrong in realistic multi-object scenes.

The comparison to VLA baselines raises fairness concerns. Some baselines use different action parameterizations, cameras, thresholds, training schedules, and checkpoint selection rules; for OpenVLA in simulation the success threshold is relaxed, while other details may still disadvantage it. The very poor OpenVLA/GROOT results are surprising and need stronger validation.

The paper repeatedly contrasts LEGO as trained from scratch or without large pretraining, but the vision stack uses MVP pretraining and SAM 2/detectors. This weakens the positioning against pretrained models and should be stated more carefully.

Real-world statistical evidence is limited. The Franka evaluation is sizable but lacks confidence intervals, per-object breakdowns, and failure analysis; the H1-2 evaluation uses only 5 trials per object and notes hardware issues, making conclusions about dexterous-hand generalization tentative.

The object generation procedure and training-object selection are somewhat confounded. The real toys are described as the 250 toys with highest simulated success rates, which may bias the distribution toward easier-to-grasp shapes rather than purely random objects.

Novelty is moderate rather than high. Object-centric manipulation, segmentation-guided pooling, primitive-based shape abstraction, and toy/synthetic data for robot learning all have substantial precedent; the contribution is mainly a useful combination with solid empirical evidence rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea.

The paper would benefit from stronger analysis of why DetPool works beyond object-background separation, including comparisons to cropped-image policies, bounding-box pooling, frozen vs fine-tuned visual encoders, and policies using only object pose/shape or depth.

strengths: The paper studies an interesting and relevant question: whether grasping policies can generalize from synthetic/random primitive-composed toys to real objects.
The experimental scope is broader than many robotics papers, including simulation, a Franka real-robot setup, a humanoid/dexterous-hand setup, robustness tests, and several ablations.
The main empirical result is potentially useful: object-centric masking/pooling appears to substantially improve zero-shot generalization over standard pooling variants in the authors' setup.
The toy-generation pipeline is simple and reasonably reproducible, and the appendices provide useful hardware, printing, data collection, and training details.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution, DetPool, is quite incremental: it uses externally provided object masks to restrict ViT attention and pool object patches. This is a plausible engineering choice, but not a conceptually strong advance for a top-tier AI venue.

The main claims are stronger than the evidence. The paper frames the result as learning to grasp anything from random toys, but evaluation is mostly tabletop pick-up of YCB-like rigid objects with known target segmentation/detection support.

The comparison to VLA baselines is not fully convincing. OpenVLA-OFT and pi0-FAST are very large generalist models whose action parameterization, inputs, training schedule, and control modes differ from LEGO; poor fine-tuning results may reflect implementation mismatch rather than a meaningful limitation of those methods.

The real Franka result does not actually beat the strongest fine-tuned baseline: pi0-FAST reaches 76.56% while LEGO reaches 66.67%. The abstract and conclusion emphasize outperforming state-of-the-art approaches, which is at best selectively true.

The method relies heavily on object masks or detectors. In simulation it uses ground-truth masks, and in real experiments it requires a trained detector plus SAM 2. This weakens the claim that the policy itself learned robust object-centric generalization.
The real-world humanoid evaluation is small: 13 objects, 5 trials each, one arm only, and acknowledged hardware issues. This is suggestive but not strong evidence for broad embodiment generalization.

The paper does not sufficiently isolate whether gains come from toy compositionality, object masking, pretrained MVP visual features, absolute joint control, or other implementation choices. Some ablations exist, but the causal story remains muddled.

The novelty of training on primitive-based synthetic/compositional objects is under-positioned relative to prior work on domain randomization, procedural object generation, primitive representations, object-centric grasping, and segmentation-based manipulation.

Several evaluation choices appear favorable to the proposed method, including ground-truth masks in simulation, lowered success threshold for OpenVLA-OFT in one setting, and selecting the 250 toys with highest simulated success rates for real printing.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite many details: the project page is blank in the extracted manuscript, and it is unclear whether code, datasets, masks, toy meshes, detector annotations, and trained checkpoints are actually available.

strengths: The paper studies an interesting and practically important question: whether grasping policies can generalize to real objects after training only on randomly composed primitive-shape toys. The framing is clear, memorable, and relevant to scalable robot learning.

The experimental scope is unusually strong for this area. The paper includes simulation, a real Franka/YCB evaluation over 64 objects with repeated placements, and an additional humanoid dexterous-hand setting, plus a push-to-target extension in the appendix.

The main empirical result is compelling: DetPool substantially improves zero-shot transfer over mean/CLS/attention pooling in simulation, reaches 80% on simulated YCB with 2500 demos, and obtains 66.7% real-world Franka success despite using a much smaller policy than VLA baselines.

The ablations are extensive and useful, covering data scaling, number/diversity of toys, primitive types, toy complexity, model size, mask noise, lighting, clutter, distractors, color diversity, control parameterization, and condition/prediction lengths.

The object-centric representation idea is simple, modular, and practically appealing. Applying an attention mask inside a ViT and pooling only target-object patches is easy to understand and could be reused in other visuomotor policies.

The manuscript gives substantial implementation detail, including toy generation, printing settings, hardware setup, teleoperation protocol, evaluation grids, and baseline training details, which improves reproducibility.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is somewhat incremental. DetPool is a straightforward combination of segmentation masks, masked attention, and object-token pooling, and the broader idea of object-centric manipulation is well established. The paper's impact therefore depends heavily on the empirical evidence.

The central claims about learning from toys are partly entangled with pretrained components. The policy uses a pretrained MVP ViT, SAM 2, and a trained detector for real settings, so claims such as training from scratch or learning generalization purely from toy demonstrations should be qualified more carefully.

The method depends on reliable target-object masks or detections at train and test time. In real experiments, the appendix describes manually annotating 200 toy images to train a Faster R-CNN detector and then using SAM 2. This extra perception pipeline is not fully accounted for in the comparison and may limit deployment in cluttered multi-object settings.

Some baseline comparisons raise fairness questions. The VLA baselines use different action/control choices in places, OpenVLA-OFT has a relaxed simulation success threshold, checkpoint selection/tuning differs across models, and the very poor performance of some strong baselines suggests possible implementation or adaptation issues. More careful matched-control baselines would strengthen the conclusions.

The real-world result is strong but not dominant: finetuned pi0-FAST outperforms LEGO on the Franka setup. The paper argues data/model efficiency, but the headline claim that LEGO outperforms state-of-the-art approaches needs to be stated with this caveat.

The real humanoid evaluation is promising but small: only 13 objects with 5 trials each, hardware issues affected the setup, and only one arm/hand was used. This supports plausibility rather than a definitive embodiment-generalization claim.

The real Franka training toys are selected as the 250 toys with highest simulated success rates, which may bias the training set toward easier-to-grasp shapes. The paper would benefit from comparing against random toy selection in the real setup.

The paper focuses mainly on single-step grasping. The push-to-target appendix helps, but the evidence for broader manipulation generalization remains limited relative to some of the broader language in the abstract and conclusion.
